paragraphs: The string was tied around its neck, between the third servo and the fourth, and the other end vanished into gray fog. The ring was where it always was, three metres of chalk on cold slate, and the pit was where it always was too, in the middle, breathing out a faint draft. Yellow Duck Sweater began walking backwards. Its knees wobbled on the slate. The string went tight. Something on the far side was walking backwards too, at exactly its speed, with exactly its small hesitations, as if it had been trained on the same seeds.

Then the fog thinned, and the duck saw two things. The other duck was the reference duck, plain white, no sweater, servos ticking in the cold. And the string was not string. It was yellow yarn, pulled loop by loop from the hem of its own sweater, which now stopped well above its belly. Every step backwards cost a row of stitches. The duck stopped. The reference duck stopped one beat later, as if it had been waiting to be asked. Neither pulled. The yarn sagged between them across the pit, low and soft, and a thin crescent moon slid down from the clouds, settled on the middle of it like a bead on a necklace, and swung there over the dark.

imagePrompt: Yellow Duck Sweater, a small two-legged tabletop robot. Its head is a smooth, chunky white plastic shell shaped like a small loaf of bread: about one and a half times as long front to back as it is tall, deep and boxy with softly rounded corners and a mostly flat top. It is not a round dome or ball, and not a long thin tube. It has an orange trim along the bottom edge and a small orange hinge on each side. At the front of the head is a single round camera eye: a black lens inside a thick orange-yellow ring. It has no beak and no mouth. The head sits on a tall, thin neck, about as tall as the head is long, made of stacked black servo motors with a few loose black wires, leaning slightly forward. Its body is a small, boxy white torso with rounded corners. It has no arms and no hands. Its short legs are black servo joints with white plastic covers on the hips, knees slightly bent. Its feet are flat and rounded like duck feet, orange on top with yellow soles. It wears a small, chunky-knit, bright lemon-yellow crewneck sweater over its white torso, slightly too big, with a ribbed collar, cuffs, and hem. Knitted into the front of the sweater is a simple cartoon duckling: pale yellow body with a thick black outline, a black dot eye, a curved line for its wing, an orange beak, and orange feet. A single full-color comic page with six panels of equal size in a grid of two columns and three rows, separated by clean white gutters, read left to right and top to bottom. The same robot duck appears in every panel and looks identical each time, unless a panel says otherwise. No speech bubbles, captions, sound effects, panel numbers, or any other text. Panel 1: In a misty gray night, the robot duck in its yellow duckling sweater stands at the edge of a round chalk ring on a cold slate floor, a thin string tied around its tall neck and stretching away into thick fog. Panel 2: In the middle of the chalk ring is a dark round pit, and a faint swirl of cool air rises out of it while the duck stands nervously at the ring's edge with its knees bent and wobbling. Panel 3: The duck walks backwards across the slate, away from the pit, as the string pulls tight into the fog, where the faint gray outline of a second duck-shaped robot can just be seen walking backwards too, two ducks in all. Panel 4: The fog has cleared and two ducks face each other across the pit: the yellow-sweater duck on one side and a plain white robot duck with no sweater on the other, the string stretched between their necks. Panel 5: Close-up of the yellow-sweater duck looking down at its own sweater, whose hem is unravelling into a single strand of yellow yarn that is the string, the sweater now noticeably shorter. Panel 6: Two ducks stand still on opposite sides of the dark pit, the yellow yarn sagging softly between them, and a thin glowing crescent moon hangs on the middle of the yarn like a bead, swinging over the darkness. Warm children's comic art: clean confident ink outlines, soft flat colors with gentle shading, a dreamy night palette, cozy and a little surreal. Friendly for an 11-year-old. No text, letters, logos, or numbers anywhere in the image. Real people do not appear.
